1.title: High-Performing Databases
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: High-Performing Databases. This module covers task statement three point three. You will choose a database type and engine from the access pattern, plan capacity, configure read replicas and connections, add caching, and plan migrations. The exam describes data and an access pattern, and asks you to choose the database.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Choose a database type and engine from the access pattern. Plan capacity: instance classes, Provisioned I O P S, capacity units and serverless scaling. Configure read replicas, endpoints and connection handling. Integrate caching with ElastiCache, Dax and MemoryDB. And pick a path for homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lantern and Loom Chooses Databases
1.text: Lantern and Loom has several data needs. Orders need transactions and S Q L. Browsing the catalog is read-heavy. Shopping carts need millisecond lookups at any scale. Recommendations follow relationships between products. And a self-managed My S Q L server on E C two must move to a managed service. Your job is to match each need to a database.

1.title: Database Types and Access Patterns
1.text: Start with the types. Relational databases, R D S and Aurora, suit transactions, joins and S Q L. Key-value and document, which is DynamoDB, gives single-digit millisecond lookups at any scale. In-memory, ElastiCache and MemoryDB, gives microsecond reads for caching and sessions. Document, DocumentDB, is MongoDB-compatible, and stores Jay-son documents. Jay-son is short for JavaScript Object Notation. Graph, Neptune, suits highly connected data. And wide-column, Keyspaces, runs Cassandra workloads. For read-intensive workloads, use replicas and caches. For write-intensive ones, use bigger instances, Provisioned I O P S, and well-spread keys. Exam tip: name the access pattern first.

1.title: Amazon RDS Engines and Capacity
1.text: Amazon R D S manages these engines: My S Q L, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, S Q L Server and D B two, plus Aurora. A W S runs backups, patching, failure detection and recovery; you tune the queries. Instance classes include D B dot M for general purpose, D B dot R, X and Z for memory, D B dot C for compute, and D B dot T for burstable. For storage, choose General Purpose S S D, or Provisioned I O P S for I O-intensive production with consistent low latency. Use Multi-A Z for availability and read replicas for reads. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, Magnetic storage is deprecated, so check the page. Exam tip: R D S is the default for relational; choose the engine your application and tools need.

1.title: Amazon Aurora
1.text: Amazon Aurora is My S Q L- and PostgreSQL-compatible. A W S cites up to six times the throughput of stock engines on similar hardware. The cluster volume grows automatically, up to two hundred fifty-six tebibytes, with data in three Availability Zones. Up to fifteen Aurora Replicas share that same storage, so lag is small, and one can take over after a failure. A reader endpoint spreads reads. And you can move from R D S My S Q L or PostgreSQL by snapshot or replication. The figure shows a writer and readers sharing a cluster volume across three zones. Exam tip: relational, My S Q L or PostgreSQL compatible, fast failover and many replicas points to Aurora.

1.title: Aurora Serverless
1.text: Aurora Serverless is an on-demand, autoscaling configuration of Aurora. Capacity is measured in Aurora capacity units, or A C U s. It scales in steps as small as half an A C U, usually without pausing transactions. You set a minimum and a maximum, and it can scale to zero with auto pause. It suits variable or unpredictable load, new applications, multi-tenant fleets, and development and test. Readers can scale on their own, and a cluster can mix serverless and provisioned instances. It works with global databases and R D S Proxy. As of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, older material separates version one and version two, so check. Exam tip: spiky or unknown load, with no wish to size instances, is Aurora Serverless.

1.title: Read Replicas, Endpoints and Connections
1.text: R D S read replicas are asynchronous copies that you create yourself; R D S does not autoscale them. Aurora Replicas share storage, and Aurora Auto Scaling can add or remove them. Send reads to the reader endpoint or the replica endpoints; the application must split reads from writes. Cross-Region replicas serve local reads and disaster recovery. Replica data can lag, so do not use it where reads must be current. And R D S Proxy pools connections, which helps Lambda and traffic spikes. Exam tip: if reads are the bottleneck, add replicas; if connections are the bottleneck, add R D S Proxy.

1.title: Amazon DynamoDB
1.text: For DynamoDB, remember these points. On-demand mode is the default and recommended option for most workloads: you pay per request, with no capacity planning. Provisioned mode has you set reads and writes per second, and suits steady, predictable load. Reads are eventually consistent by default. Strongly consistent reads cost twice as much, and are not available on global secondary indexes. A well-spread partition key avoids hot partitions. Global tables give multi-Region, multi-active replicas, and as of the fifth of November, twenty twenty-six, they also offer strong consistency across Regions as an option. Exam tip: unknown traffic is on-demand; steady, forecastable traffic is provisioned.

1.title: Caching with ElastiCache, DAX and MemoryDB
1.text: Three in-memory services appear. Amazon ElastiCache is an in-memory store for Val key, Redis O S S and Memcached, serverless or node-based. Use it as a cache in front of any database, or for sessions and leaderboards. DynamoDB Accelerator, or Dax, is a DynamoDB-compatible cache with microsecond reads of eventually consistent data. Use it for read-heavy tables with hot keys, not for write-heavy tables or strongly consistent reads. Amazon MemoryDB is a durable in-memory database, with a Multi-A Z transaction log. Use it as a primary database that needs microsecond speed. Exam tip: a cache in front of a database is ElastiCache or Dax; a durable in-memory primary is MemoryDB.

1.title: Purpose-Built Databases
1.text: Several purpose-built databases fill gaps. Amazon DocumentDB is a document database that is MongoDB-compatible. Storage grows automatically, with up to fifteen replicas and data in three zones. Amazon Neptune is a graph database, using Gremlin, open Cypher and S P A R Q L, for recommendations, fraud detection and knowledge graphs. Amazon Keyspaces is wide-column and Cassandra-compatible, and serverless, so you run existing Cassandra code. And Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics on large data; module thirteen covers it. Exam tip: match the data model: documents, graph, Cassandra or warehouse.

2.title: Migrating Databases
2.text: There are two kinds of migration. A homogeneous migration keeps the same engine, such as My S Q L to R D S or Aurora My S Q L. Use snapshots, native tools, replication, or D M S. A heterogeneous migration changes engines, such as Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL. Convert the schema with D M S Schema Conversion or the A W S Schema Conversion Tool, and then D M S moves the data. A W S D M S runs one-time migrations or ongoing replication, so the source can stay online until cutover. D M S Fleet Advisor inventories databases to plan. Data is encrypted at rest and in flight. Exam tip: same engine uses native tools; a different engine means convert the schema, then D M S.

2.title: Choosing a Database
2.text: Here is the decision path. Relational data with transactions goes to R D S or Aurora. Key-value lookups at massive scale go to DynamoDB. Microsecond reads go to ElastiCache, Dax or MemoryDB. Relationships go to Neptune. And MongoDB or Cassandra code goes to DocumentDB or Keyspaces. The figure shows a decision path from the shape of the data to the matching database. Exam tip: the access pattern, not the brand, picks the database.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: High-Performing Databases
2.text: Here is what the exam asks. Which database type for the data and access pattern. Which engine or compatibility: My S Q L, PostgreSQL, Oracle or S Q L Server. Which capacity approach: Provisioned I O P S, on-demand, provisioned or serverless. Which replica or cache removes the bottleneck. And which migration path: homogeneous or heterogeneous. Exam tip: underline read-heavy, write-heavy, spiky, relational or connected.

2.title: Design Check: Lantern and Loom Chooses Databases
2.text: Here is the Design Check. Cover the right column and answer each row yourself. Orders with transactions and S Q L: Aurora. Browsing overloads the primary: Aurora Replicas behind the reader endpoint, plus a cache. Carts need millisecond lookups: DynamoDB on-demand. A few hot product keys: Dax in front of DynamoDB. Spiky weekend load on a new database: Aurora Serverless. Recommendations from relationships: Amazon Neptune. And moving the self-managed My S Q L: Aurora My S Q L, by snapshot or replication.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. The types are relational, key-value, in-memory, document, graph and wide-column. For relational, R D S is the default, Aurora adds scale and fast failover, and Serverless handles spiky load. For DynamoDB, on-demand suits unknown load, provisioned suits steady load, and Dax speeds hot reads. To scale reads, use replicas, the reader endpoint, caches and R D S Proxy. And to migrate, use native tools for the same engine, and schema conversion plus D M S for a different one.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Lantern and Loom's order system needs a managed relational database compatible with My S Q L, with fast failover, storage that grows automatically and many read replicas. Which service fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Amazon Aurora My S Q L-Compatible Edition. DynamoDB is key-value, Neptune is a graph database, and ElastiCache is an in-memory cache.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. The shopping-cart service of Lantern and Loom needs single-digit millisecond lookups by cart I D, traffic that is unpredictable, and no capacity planning. Which design fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: a DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode. It scales automatically for unpredictable traffic with no capacity planning.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A small set of popular products at Lantern and Loom is read thousands of times a second from a DynamoDB table, and slightly stale data is acceptable. The team wants microsecond reads with minimal code change. What should the architect add? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: a DynamoDB Accelerator, or Dax, cluster. It is a DynamoDB-compatible in-memory cache that serves eventually consistent reads in microseconds.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A new reporting database at Lantern and Loom will have an unknown, spiky load for its first months, and the team does not want to choose an instance size. Which option fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Aurora Serverless with a minimum and a maximum capacity. It adjusts capacity in small steps, so you pay for what the workload uses and need not guess an instance size.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Select two. Which two statements about Amazon DynamoDB are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. On-demand mode is the recommended default, and reads from global secondary indexes are always eventually consistent. Eventually consistent reads cost half as much, provisioned mode charges for the capacity provisioned, and Dax suits read-heavy tables.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Lantern and Loom must move an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime. Which approach fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: convert the schema, then migrate with D M S and ongoing replication. Moving between different engines is a heterogeneous migration.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: B. Question two: A. Question three: D. Question four: C. Question five: A and C. Question six: B. In Module nine, we design high-performing network architectures.
